summary: Introduces terminology to categorize types of YANG modules. YANG is used by many organizations, but there was no well-known vocabulary for the kinds of modules. Consistent terms help analysis and discussion between groups.

eli5.summary: Sorting toys into labelled boxes needs names for the boxes. This gives names to the kinds of YANG modules.

questions: how do you categorize yang modules
subtitle: A common language for categorizing data modeling modules.

tldr.problem: Organizations worldwide use YANG modules for data modeling, but there was no standard vocabulary to classify and discuss different types of modules, making it hard to analyze and compare approaches.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines two classification dimensions: abstraction layers (Network Service modules vs. Network Element modules) and origin types (Standard, Vendor-Specific, and User-Specific).
tldr.outcome: A common taxonomy helps SDOs, vendors, operators, and orchestrators understand module relationships and choose the right module for their needs.

today: RFC 8199 is an Informational RFC published in July 2017 and remains the standard reference for YANG module classification across the industry.

sections.title: The Need for Module Classification
sections.content:
The YANG data modeling language has become widely adopted by standards organizations, vendors, open-source projects, and enterprises for managing network device configuration and state. However, as adoption grew, there was no consistent way to categorize or discuss the different types of YANG modules being created, making it difficult for operators to understand which modules were appropriate for their use and for standards bodies to coordinate development efforts.

This RFC provides a shared vocabulary for classifying YANG modules along two dimensions: their abstraction layer (how they represent data, from specific devices to abstract services) and their origin (whether they come from standards bodies, vendors, or users). A common taxonomy benefits operators choosing modules, vendors explaining their products, and engineers across organizations working on similar problems.
sections.eli5: Different people building with YANG modules needed a common way to describe what kind of module they had and what it was for. This RFC gave them that shared language.

sections.title: Two Abstraction Layers
sections.content:
YANG modules sit at two distinct abstraction levels. Network Element YANG Modules describe a single device's configuration, features, and capabilities—things like OSPF routing, interface settings, or ACL rules. Network Service YANG Modules describe abstract network services (like Layer 2 or Layer 3 VPN) that an orchestrator can decompose into device-level configurations. A Network Service module specifies the high-level intent, while orchestration logic translates that into specific commands to multiple Network Element modules.

This two-level separation allows for reuse: a Network Service module can compose existing Network Element modules in different ways, while multiple teams can develop at each layer independently. Network Element modules benefit from teams with deep protocol expertise, while Network Service modules benefit from operators experienced in service design.
sections.eli5: One layer describes what a single device can do. The other describes a whole service across many devices. Splitting this way lets different experts work on different pieces.

sections.title: Three Origin Types
sections.content:
Standard YANG Modules are published by standards development organizations such as the IETF or IEEE, following formal processes. They are not tied to any specific product version. Vendor-Specific YANG Modules are developed by equipment vendors, consortia, or open-source projects to support their own implementations; their lifecycles align with product releases. User-Specific YANG Modules are created by operators to express their own needs beyond what standards or vendors provide, often to model local policies or services.

These origin types can coexist in a single deployment. For instance, a vendor might publish a standard module, extend it with vendor-specific enhancements using YANG's augment mechanism, and then an operator might further extend it with user-specific modules. Understanding which origin a module comes from helps operators assess maturity, compatibility, and support expectations.
sections.eli5: Modules come from three places: official standards groups, companies, or an organization's own team. Each has different update schedules and stability guarantees.

sections.title: How the Classification Works Together
sections.content:
The two dimensions combine to give a complete picture. A standard L3VPN module from the IETF is a Standard Network Service Module—it describes a VPN service in a vendor-neutral way. A router vendor's module describing BGP on their specific hardware is a Vendor-Specific Network Element Module. An enterprise's module that adds proprietary service tags to a standard module is a User-Specific extension. Looking at the origin-type diagram, a single standard base module can have vendor and user extensions augmenting it, building up capabilities in layers.

This classification helps operators understand what they're working with. When choosing modules for a service, they can identify which modules serve their purpose, understand the implications of each origin type, and plan how to compose them. Standards bodies can see which areas need better standard coverage. Equipment vendors can explain how their offerings relate to standards.
sections.eli5: By knowing both what level it works at and where it came from, you understand everything you need about a module.
